item.title: Community-Engaged and Community-Partnered Research — Fri Oct 30, 9:30 AM — None
item.description:
REGISTRATION: Click Here
Engaging and partnering with community members and entities in research, sometimes in the form of research practice partnership, can be a powerful mechanism for ensuring research is appropriately situated within the context and utilized for social change. These concepts and processes are highly complex, and often quite challenging, both in theory and in practice. This session will introduce the meaning of "community-engaged research" and related terms, explore their relevance for both researchers and communities, and consider recommendations for enacting best practices.
This event is only open to current Duke faculty, staff, and students. Attending this event fulfills the RCR-200 requirement for Faculty and Staff as well as the 714 RCR credit for graduate students, but participants must attend for at least 60 minutes to receive credit.
Source: Duke University

item.title: SSRI Workshop: Community-Engaged and Community-Partnered Research — Fri Oct 30, 9:30 AM — None
item.description:
Zoom https://duke.zoom.us/j/95423397959
Community-engaged and community-partnered research can help ensure that research is grounded in context and positioned to contribute to meaningful social change. At the same time, building effective research partnerships with communities can be complex.
This workshop introduces key concepts and approaches to community-engaged research, including research-practice partnerships. Participants will consider why these approaches matter, how they can benefit both researchers and communities, and recommendations for putting best practices into action.
Topics include:
Defining community-engaged and community-partnered research Understanding related approaches and terminology The value of research partnerships for researchers and communities Common challenges in community-engaged research Recommendations and best practices for building effective partnerships
Source: Duke University

item.title: Coordination as the First Principle of Intelligence? Human Agency and the Future of AI — Fri Oct 30, 11:00 AM — None
item.description:
What principles make human intelligence distinctive, and to what extent can we recreate them in artificial systems? Contemporary AI has largely pursued intelligence through optimization-first, individual-first principles: systems are trained in isolation from other agents to optimize specified objectives-maximizing reward in reinforcement learning or predicting the next token in large language models. Systems built on these principles have achieved superhuman performance in many individual problem-solving domains and have fueled the hypothesis that continued scaling is sufficient for artificial general intelligence encompassing all aspects of human intelligence. On this view, even uniquely human social intelligence should emerge once systems optimize an appropriately aligned objective.

The son of immigrants from Michoacán, Mexico, who settled in East Palo Alto in the 1980s, he was the first in his family to graduate from college. After Duke, he earned degrees from Rutgers-Newark (MFA), the University of Oxford (MPhil), where he studied as a Marshall Scholar, and Stanford University (PhD in Modern Thought and Literature). item.title: The Role of Community Self Reliance in Black Agrarianism — Fri Oct 30, 3:00 PM — Duke Campus Farm
item.description:
The RePlant team is kicking off this year's Composting Theory workshop series with "The Role of Community Self Reliance in Black Agrarianism." Raquel Douglas (Brown University) and Mama Dorathy Barker of Olusanya Farm will be leading a two-part workshop on Friday, October 30th, 3-6pm at the Duke Campus Farm's Cackalacky Heritage Garden.
Practices of self-reliance and interdependence are woven through the centuries-long timeline of Black farming and foodways in North Carolina. It's how elders made ways out of no way, how they fought food apartheid, and what many elders desire for future generations. It's a land-based cultural practice of agency and resistance.
This two-part workshop will include oral histories, a hands-on herb and flower preservation demonstration led by Mama Barker (3-4:30pm open to all), followed by a discussion of Raquel's Black Agrarian Soul, which theorizes how North Carolina Black farmers understand the cultural, political, and spiritual significance of farming

item.title: Adaptive Bayesian Estimation of Conditional Densities Based on Orthogonal Polynomials — Fri Oct 30, 3:30 PM — Old Chemistry 116
item.description: This paper develops a nonparametric Bayesian model for conditional densities based on orthogonal polynomial series. The conditional density is the square of the series divided by its conditional integral; the specification has a closed-form likelihood and does not require modeling the covariate distribution. A normalization that fixes the conditional mean of the series identifies the representation and makes the map from coefficients to densities Lipschitz in Hellinger distance. For a prior on smoothness, the number of terms, and the coefficients, the posterior contracts at the minimax rate in covariate-averaged Hellinger distance, without a logarithmic factor. A matching lower bound is established in the conditional problem. Further results cover conditional distribution functions and quantiles, densities that may vanish, and selection of polynomial terms. item.title: Musicology Lecture: Andrea Bohlman, UNC-Chapel Hill — Fri Oct 30, 4:00 PM — Biddle Music Building
item.description:
"Pressing Pause At Lunch (ca. 1955): An Estranged Listening to Food and Tape"
A fisherman croons opera into a restaurant's mic in Marseilles, France; a Black domestic worker sings after serving lunch to white visitors at a summer estate in Virginia; in rural Poland a group of women is at work harvesting potatoes while a neighbor sings in the adjacent field. The scenes of music history (and music in history) I read closely here are not patently connected, except that each occurred in the mid-1950s, each links the practices of making/consuming food with musicking, and each was recorded on magnetic tape. I wonder what, bearing in mind our present moments' critical concern with global media's transnational corporate entanglements and extractive infrastructures, we might learn from sitting with and connecting these moments that, in my analysis, show the limits of (tape) recording.

item.title: CAMEH Friday Fora — Fri Oct 30, 4:30 PM — John Hope Franklin Center
item.description:
Preeti Singh is Assistant Professor of Asian and Middle Eastern Studies at Duke University, USA. She is a scholar of postcolonial literature and theory and South Asian cultural studies. Her current book project reads the aesthetics and politics of the Indian National Emergency (1975-1977) at the intersection of decolonization and the global Cold War. Her second project conceptualizes decolonization as a planetary phenomenon with attention to the aesthetics of alignment, solidarity, and indigeneity across the Global South in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Her wider research and teaching interests include political theory, South-South solidarities, and the urban and environmental humanities. Her writing has appeared or is forthcoming in South Asian Review, Philosophy and Global Affairs, Global South Studies, The International Journal of Comic Art, Public Books, and Modern Fiction Studies.

item.title: What Enterprise AI Looks Like When It Works — Wed Nov 4, 11:00 AM
item.description:
All Things AI (Live) In this session of *Newsweek’s* “AI Impact Forum,” **Dr. Ranjit Tinaikar** sits down with **Firdaus Bhathena**, executive vice president and chief technology and transformation officer at S&P Global, to examine what it takes to turn advances in AI into meaningful business impact. Drawing on Bhathena's experience leading technology and transformation at S&P Global and previously at FIS Global and CVS Health, the conversation will explore why trusted, differentiated data becomes increasingly important as powerful AI models become more widely available—and what companies need to do to put that data to work. Bhathena and Tinaikar will discuss moving beyond experimentation, making data governed and reusable, redesigning workflows around new capabilities and balancing speed with trust, security and resilience. They will also examine how leaders can keep technology initiatives focused on customer problems and identify where genuine competitive advantage can emerge.

item.title: FOA Annual Meeting: Remembering the American Revolution in the Cherokee Homeland — Wed Nov 4, 2:00 PM
item.description:
FOA Annual Meeting & Program presentation this year is Remembering the American Revolution in the Cherokee Homeland.
Commemorating the American Revolution poses particular challenges if one lives in far Western North Carolina. Here in the Cherokee ancestral homelands, the Revolution brought a bitter and destructive conflict over Cherokee land, with a portion of the Cherokee population entering the war as members of a British-allied coalition of Indigenous peoples. That war, in turn, belonged to a much longer struggle to protect Cherokee land and the wellbeing of Cherokee communities – a struggle that preceded the Revolution and continued long after 1776. In this presentation, Shana Bushyhead Condill (Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians), Executive Director of the Museum of the Cherokee People, and Andrew Denson, professor of history at Western Carolina University, will discuss the challenges involved in remembering the Revolution in the mountain region. item.description:
Data Science Raleigh As enterprises move from isolated AI assistants to interconnected agentic systems, orchestration is becoming a critical layer of the AI stack. Coordinating multiple agents across tools, data sources, models, and workflows introduces new opportunities for automation—but also new challenges around reliability, governance, observability, and control.
This session explores what it takes to design and operationalize agent orchestration in enterprise environments. item.title: Kudzu and Wisteria Basket Weaving — Sun Nov 29, 10:00 AM — Duke Gardens–Pelham-Cullen Classroom in the Barnes Welcome Center
item.description: Learn to weave a basket with kudzu and wisteria, invasive species that grow quickly and plentifully throughout the Southeast, with instructor Angela Eastman of Flag Mountain Studio. The mature vines of both plants can be harvested and processed into bark strips and woody material that form the structure for strong and beautiful baskets. In learning traditional wicker weaving techniques to work with this plentiful material, you’ll connect to a long human lineage of working with natural materials to create useful vessels. You can expect to leave with a small basket or platter woven from kudzu and wisteria. Throughout the day together, as you build creative community and ecological awareness, Angela will invite a new way to understand “weeds” in the environment where they live, shifting perspectives to view these plants as creative collaborators and resourceful cohabiters. item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Wed Jan 27, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources
